title: Empirical Integration of a Formal Network Verifier as an Oracle inside an LLM Generate–Verify–Repair Loop: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired within‑task experiment (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) that tests whether embedding a formal network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) loop increases detection/rejection of unsafe or incorrect LLM‑generated network configurations and improves bounded repair success versus single‑shot generation. Using a synthetic intent→configuration suite (N=270 tasks: 3 vendor syntaxes × 3 topology templates × 30 tasks), gpt-5-mini as generator, and a deterministic netops validator/emulator as ground truth, we observed that the generator produced verifier‑acceptable candidates for every task. Baseline (single‑shot) accepted 270/270 (100%); guarded (verify → optional bounded repair) accepted 270/270 (100%). Verifier rejections: 0/270; bounded repair calls invoked: 0; repair successes conditional on initial reject: 0/0. Paired difference = 0.00 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00], exact McNemar two‑sided p=1.0). On the preregistered validation subset (54 tasks) verifier–emulator concordance was 54/54 (false_accept=0, false_reject=0). All preregistered artifacts, model traces, scoring JSONs, and hashes (see execution/*) are released; we interpret the null result with respect to shared‑initial generation semantics, task difficulty, verifier design, and bounded repair budget and outline reproducible next steps.

sections.introduction: Motivation and question. Natural‑language intent→configuration pipelines driven by large language models (LLMs) promise simpler NetOps but raise correctness and safety concerns: stochastic generation can produce syntactically plausible but semantically unsafe device commands. A common operational mitigation is a Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) architecture: a generative model proposes a configuration, a deterministic verifier rejects unsafe candidates, and a repair loop attempts bounded automatic fixes informed by verifier diagnostics. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment to ask: does embedding a formal network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded GVR loop (single bounded repair attempt per rejected candidate) increase detection/rejection of unsafe or incorrect LLM‑generated configurations and improve bounded repair success versus single‑shot generation? Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired empirical run with complete provenance and artifact hashes (preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e…; master‑prompt archived — provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 1872df1e…). (2) A synthetic intent→configuration task suite and a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet emulator + deterministic netops validator used as executable ground truth. (3) Open release of generation traces, verifier traces, scoring JSONs, the execution manifest, and analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and follow‑up studies.
sections.related_work: Positioning. We situate this experiment amid GVR and verifier‑in‑the‑loop work for safety‑critical generation (cf. Cadenas’ GVR framing [doi:10.2139/ssrn.6754899]) and formal network verification literature (e.g., quantitative NetKAT analyses [doi:10.1145/3808318]). Surveys and recent agentic NetOps work motivate task design and verifier semantics (see cited records). Unlike broad model benchmarking, our study is an operational, preregistered test of a verifier oracle’s marginal effect in a controlled paired design with deterministic ground truth and full artifact provenance.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and freeze. We froze the experimental plan before observing outcomes (preregistration JSON keyed by study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1; SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e…). Key choices recorded in the preregistration: paired within‑task design, primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation=false), bounded repair budget (max 1 repair call per rejected candidate), fixed deterministic prompt templates, and exact analysis procedures (exact McNemar two‑sided test, paired bootstrap CIs with 10k resamples, seed=1729). Tasks and sampling. N=270 distinct intent→configuration tasks constructed as 3 vendor‑style syntaxes × 3 topology templates × 30 tasks per cell. A 20% stratified validation subset (54 tasks) was reserved to compute verifier vs emulator concordance. Models and prompts. Primary generator: gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). Model configuration and settings are archived in execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Execution semantics. Per the preregistration we used shared_initial_candidate semantics: the same single generated candidate was evaluated under both baseline and guarded arms for each task, hence one generation per pair. Consequence: model_calls_used=270 (one generation per pair), which is recorded in execution/execution_manifest.json. Verifier and emulator. A deterministic netops validator/emulator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) running in Dockerized Kathará/Mininet provided ground truth intent‑constraint checks and simulated device state; validator traces and scoring JSONs are archived under execution/scoring/. Outcome measures and analysis. Primary outcomes: (a) whether the verifier rejects initial candidates (count and proportion), (b) whether bounded repair produces a verifier‑accepted configuration conditional on initial reject (repair success probability). Primary statistical test: paired binary comparison (exact McNemar two‑sided) and paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10k resamples, seed=1729). All analysis code and artifacts are archived (analysis/*). Contamination and reproducibility. Deterministic SHA‑256 snapshotting of all prompts, generated candidates, per‑call traces, and artifacts prevented silent contamination; execution manifest records per‑artifact hashes and provider‑call logs.
sections.results: Execution fidelity. All 540 planned episodes (270 pairs) completed; execution manifest and per‑episode artifacts are archived (execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/*; full hash manifest included). Model calls. Because of shared_initial_candidate semantics the experiment used one initial generation per task pair (model_calls_used = 270), not two; model configuration is archived (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2…). Primary numeric outcomes (artifact‑backed facts). Baseline accepted (verifier‑accepted initial candidate): 270/270 = 100%. Guarded accepted (generate → verifier → optional bounded repair): 270/270 = 100%. Verifier rejected initial candidate: 0/270. Bounded repair calls invoked (guarded arm): 0. Repair successes conditional on initial reject: 0/0 (no repair attempts were invoked). Paired contingency: n11=270, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Statistical inference (preregistered analysis). Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples; seed=1729). Verifier–emulator concordance (validation subset). On the preregistered validation subset of 54 tasks the verifier verdicts matched emulator ground truth for all checked cases: concordance 54/54 (false_accept = 0; false_reject = 0). Representative artifacts (examples). Representative scoring JSONs and response traces are archived (paths and SHA‑256s): execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (sha350bfaa2eec0deb0e16121f5e7effa2d8743d28f3f014856107acfabbb42d87e), execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (sha f8de4d6e1a625e42ba4907440b4377c78949ed56446e5c73030bc267e56abfaf). The full per‑artifact hash manifest and provider call traces are available in execution/execution_manifest.json (see evidence bundle).
sections.discussion: Empirical interpretation. The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one initial generation per pair; in this observed regime the generator consistently produced verifier‑acceptable candidates, so the verifier never rejected an initial candidate and the bounded repair path was never exercised. Thus the inserted verifier produced no measurable marginal effect under these exact experimental conditions; this is an evidence‑backed null result. This outcome does not imply the verifier is universally unnecessary—utility depends on (i) the generator’s sampling behavior (temperature and independent resampling vs shared candidate semantics), (ii) task hardness and adversarial/out‑of‑distribution inputs, (iii) verifier conservatism/coverage, and (iv) repair budget and repair‑prompt design. Methodological lesson: the shared‑initial generation choice was preregistered and is the principal cause of model_calls_used=270; it measures the verifier’s marginal effect on the same generated candidate rather than on independently sampled per‑condition generations. Operational implications and reproducible next steps. To evaluate verifier utility under realistic LLM variability we recommend reproducible follow‑ups that (a) use independent_condition_generation (fresh generation per condition), (b) vary model sampling temperature to expose stochastic failure modes, (c) test adversarial or OOD intents, (d) broaden models (multiple LLM families), and (e) vary verifier rule‑set conservatism and repair budgets. All procedures and artifacts in this paper enable exact replication and such follow‑ups; the execution manifest records per‑call traces and per‑artifact SHA‑256 hashes to support deterministic recomputation. Threats to validity. Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally reduced generation variability; this choice is documented and discussed as a core design decision. Construct validity: synthetic tasks approximate but do not fully replicate production NetOps complexity. External validity: single model (gpt-5-mini), synthetic task suite, single verifier variant—results are not guaranteed to generalize beyond this regime. Conclusion validity: the paired design and preregistered analysis were executed as planned and the deterministic reconciliation confirms accounting; the null result is therefore a valid empirical statement about the executed conditions.
sections.conclusion: We ran a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired experiment to test whether embedding a formal network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded GVR loop increases detection/rejection of unsafe or incorrect LLM‑generated network configurations and improves bounded repair success. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics, with gpt-5-mini and the described synthetic task suite, the generator produced verifier‑acceptable candidates for all N=270 tasks and the verifier/repair path was never invoked; both baseline and guarded arms accepted 270/270 (100%), giving a paired difference of 0.00 (95% CI [0.00,0.00], McNemar p=1.0). We release the full preregistration, model traces, scoring artifacts, validator traces, and hash manifest to enable reproducible follow‑ups that vary generation semantics, model sampling, verifier rule sets, and repair budgets. Null results reported with full provenance identify the experimental regimes where an operational intervention (here, an inserted verifier + bounded repair) does or does not alter outcomes; they therefore help prioritize future evaluations toward the regimes that matter in production NetOps.

Verifier and emulator: a deterministic netops validator/emulator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) running in Dockerized Kathará/Mininet images provided ground‑truth intent‑constraint checks; all validator traces and scoring JSONs are archived under execution/scoring/ (representative artifact: execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json sha350bfaa2eec0deb0e16121f5e7effa2d8743d28f3f014856107acfabbb42d87e). Verifier concordance: on the preregistered reserved validation subset (54 tasks) verifier verdicts matched emulator ground truth for all checked cases: verifier false‑accept = 0, verifier false‑reject = 0, concordance 54/54 (see execution/scoring/). Autonomous execution: after the autonomy lock the system performed literature review, final research‑question selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, autonomous peer review and revision, manuscript drafting, and compilation; no human manually edited or rewrote the manuscript content after the autonomy lock. Human role: the human Research Director approved the initial high‑level topic family and pre‑lock infrastructure development; no post‑lock manual manuscript editing, result alteration, or selective improvement by humans occurred. Technical restarts/deviations: the execution manifest reports completion without infrastructure restarts that altered the scientific design; all execution timestamps and per‑artifact SHA‑256 hashes are recorded and released. Limits and scope: this study used a single hosted LLM (gpt-5-mini), a synthetic intent→configuration suite, shared‑initial‑generation semantics, a bounded repair budget (maximum 1 repair call per rejected candidate), and a deterministic validator/emulator for ground truth; these methodological choices and their consequences are declared and discussed in the manuscript. Availability: all preregistration, execution, analysis artifacts, and the full hash manifest are released with the manuscript (paths and SHA‑256s appear in the supplied evidence bundle: see execution/execution_manifest.json).
limitations: Synthetic task suite and limited operational realism: results may not generalize to complex, noisy, adversarial, or production NetOps environments.
Single‑model evaluation: only gpt-5-mini was tested; results do not imply multi‑model generality.

Shared‑initial_generation semantics: both arms evaluated the same initial generated candidate (independent_condition_generation=false). This preregistered choice produced model_calls_used=270 (one initial generation per pair) and constrains interpretation: the experiment measures the verifier's marginal effect on the same generated candidate rather than the effect under independently sampled per‑condition generations.
Bounded repair budget: the repair loop allowed at most one repair call per rejected candidate; multi‑step or larger budgets were not evaluated and could change outcomes.

Verifier rule‑set sensitivity: we tested a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); different verifier conservatism or rule‑sets may change false‑accept/reject trade‑offs and observed utility.
Emulator vs production gap: emulator‑validated safety does not guarantee identical behavior on heterogeneous vendor devices or live production networks.
